Lisbon's tram network turns 150

By Marta Ribeiro — 12 March 2024

Lisbon put its first passenger tram into service in 1873, when horse-drawn carriages began running along the riverfront. One hundred and fifty years later the network is still moving people through streets that were never designed for vehicles of any kind, and the yellow trams have become the single most recognisable image of the Portuguese capital.

A network built for hills

The system covers six lines and roughly thirty one kilometres of track. Route 28 is the best known of them; it opened in 1914 and climbs from Martim Moniz through Graca and Alfama before descending again towards Campo de Ourique. Its gradients reach thirteen and a half percent, steep enough that the line still needs vehicles built specifically for it rather than the modern low-floor cars used elsewhere in the city.

Carris, the municipal operator, reports that the tram network carried twenty five million passengers in 2023. That figure is the highest recorded since the 1980s, and it represents an increase of eleven percent over the previous year.

The Remodelado fleet

Fifty eight trams are currently in service. Forty five of them are Remodelado cars, a design first built in the 1930s and rebuilt in the mid 1990s with new motors, brakes and controllers while keeping the original wooden bodywork. The remaining thirteen are articulated Siemens units introduced in 1995, which run only on the flatter coastal route between Praca da Figueira and Alges.

Maintaining the older cars is slow work. Carris keeps a dedicated workshop at Santo Amaro where bodywork is repaired by hand, and the operator says a full overhaul of a single Remodelado takes around four months.

Pressure from tourism

Route 28 has become a problem of its own success. Residents along the line report waiting for three or four full trams before being able to board, and the operator has introduced a separate tourist service, the Hills Tramcar Tour, in an attempt to absorb some of the demand. A single ride bought on board costs three euros and twenty cents, roughly double the fare paid with a rechargeable Navegante card.

What comes next

Carris has ordered ten new vehicles for delivery in 2026, the first entirely new tram design the city has bought since 1995. They will be assembled in Portugal and will run on the coastal route, releasing older articulated cars for use on the hill lines. The operator has said that the Remodelado fleet itself will not be retired, because no modern vehicle currently on the market can handle the gradients of Route 28.
